content.text: "Mother died today or yesterday maybe. I don't know"
The story is centered around Meursault, our protagonist, and is narrated in first person which gives us a peek into the mind of Camus - the same person who popularized,
"The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a human heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy."

Meursault has been in the search of meaning. He doesn't believe it fit to turn to god as everyother person does – neither he is looking for an alternative explanation per se. He has a sense of acceptedness of this absurdity, of this tussle for meaning with the universe.

Unlike other people who might use this absurdity as an excuse for shredding moral responsibilities and any notion of vice or virtue, Mersault simply exists as he is. He doesn't lie about his feelings, nor does he feels any responsibility to act in consonance with what others would want him to do. The is the prelude to the opening where, the death of his mother doesn't make him mourn like everyone else did; he simply stands there smoking a cigarette and then walks away without looking back even once. His mind is unfettered by the social or emotional sanctions.

Later, when he's standing in a courtroom after mistakenly murdering a person in the 'discomfort' due to the scorching Algerian sun, he is not tainted by the need to be saved. He doesn't care if people will understand his circumstances.
The Judge offers him a crucifix which he denies to take owing to his 'fidelity' to the absurdness and unwillingness to substitute it. The judge is horrified and terms him,

He is sentenced to death not because he killed a guy but because he didn't fit into the social edifice that makes it necessary to draw a meaning out of every event which muddles the reality. At the end of the story, while looking out of the window of his prison cell, he says,

"Gazing up at the dark sky spangled with signs and stars, for the first time, the first, I laid my heart open to the benign indifference of the universe. To feel it so like myself, so like a brother, really, I saw that I had been happy, and that I was happy still."
